text: Got the offer letter this morning. I read it three times in the parking lot and then called Ma before I'd even started the car.
Sunny walk to the bakery, warm bread, the cat followed me halfway down the street. Small day, good day.
Ravi and I finally fixed the leaking tap ourselves. Took two hours and one YouTube video but we did it and we were ridiculous about how proud we were.
Laughed so hard at dinner with Ines and Tomás that the waiter came over to check on us.
Grandpa remembered my name today without me telling him. He held my hand the whole visit. I'm still smiling.
The tomatoes on the balcony are actually turning red. I genuinely did not believe this would happen.
Saturday market with Aiko. We bought too many peaches and ate them on the steps of the library like kids.
My code passed review on the first try. Femi left a comment that just said 'clean'. Best word.
Joon-ho taught me the right way to fold dumplings and mine finally looked like dumplings instead of tiny crime scenes.
Got the bike back from the repair shop. Rode the long way home along the canal just because I could.
Snow day! Office closed. Hot chocolate, blanket, old movies with Mateo.
I'd been dreading the dentist all week and it was fine, no cavities. The relief turned into a really good mood that lasted all afternoon.
Our team won the five-a-side final. Kwame scored in the last minute and we piled on him like puppies.
Found twenty euros in last winter's coat. Bought flowers for the flat.
Dinner at Noor's. Her mother kept piling food onto my plate and calling me 'beta'. I felt like family.
The new album from my favourite band came out at midnight and it's even better than I hoped. Listened twice through on the walk to work.
Beach with the kids. Zara built a 'castle' that was mostly one wall and named it after the dog. Perfect afternoon.
Not a huge feeling, just pleasant. Coffee was good, inbox was quiet, I left on time.
The landlord agreed to fix the heating AND knocked a bit off the rent for the trouble. I did a little victory lap around the living room.
Played piano for an hour without checking my phone once. Forgot how much I love this.
Wedding rehearsal for Priya and Sean. Everything went wrong in the funniest ways and nobody cared. I love these people.
Coach Ndlovu said I can play in Saturday's match. I've been on the bench all season!
Video call with Abuela. She showed me her new glasses and her terrible jokes have gotten worse, which I love.
Sometimes the day just clicks. Got through my list, went for a run, cooked properly. I feel really good.
Elif surprised me with tickets to the jazz club. We stayed until they turned the lights on.
Rain all day but the house smelled like cinnamon rolls and Marcus played records. Cosy and happy.
Yesterday I was a mess about the presentation. Today it went great and three people asked for my slides. What a difference a day makes.
Puppy class graduation. Biscuit did NOT sit on command but he did steal the trainer's hat and everyone clapped anyway.
Kids' drawing on the fridge says 'best mum in the univers'. Leaving the spelling exactly as it is forever.
I keep replaying the moment Ana said yes. We're getting married. WE'RE GETTING MARRIED.
Morning run in the fog, then a long shower, then the crossword with Pete. A soft, happy Sunday.
I was worried the reunion would be awkward. It wasn't at all. Like no time had passed. Came home buzzing.
Lunch in the sun with Daniela and Chiara, gelato after. Didn't check email for an hour and the world survived.
Dad finally tried the curry I've been perfecting and asked for seconds. He never asks for seconds.
Kofi got the scholarship. I've been helping him with applications for months and when he called he could barely talk.
Long weekend in the hills. Woodsmoke, terrible card games, Lucía's awful singing. I want to bottle this.
Today was the first day since the breakup that I felt genuinely happy, not just fine. Noticed it on the tram and nearly laughed out loud.
Spent the evening on the roof with Yusuf watching the meteor shower. We counted 23. He made a wish every single time.
Took Nana to the seaside like she's been asking. She ate chips on the wall and told stories about being nineteen. Golden.
Our little choir sang at the care home. One woman sang along to every word with her eyes closed.
The plant I thought I'd killed has a new leaf. Hello, little guy.
We cooked together for once instead of eating on the sofa. Talked about everything. This is what I want more of.
Results day: 2:1. Not the first I dreamed of but I'm honestly thrilled, and Mum's been crying happy tears all afternoon.
Picnic in the park with the whole cousin crowd. Uncle Raj brought his ancient guitar. Best afternoon of the year so far.
Mochi died this morning. Fourteen years. The house is so quiet I keep hearing her collar that isn't there.
Didn't get the job. They said it was close. Somehow that makes it worse.
Packed up Dad's study today. His reading glasses were still on the desk folded like he'd be right back.
Grey day, grey mood. Nothing is wrong exactly. I just feel low and heavy.
Leila and I officially ended things. It was kind and mutual and I still cried on the bus home.
The café where I wrote my whole thesis is closing next month. Silly to feel this much about a café.
Watched Ben's train pull out. Six months until I see him again. Walked home the long way so I wouldn't have to be in the flat yet.
I found out Amara's mum passed away last week and nobody told me. I would have gone to the funeral.
Woke up crying from a dream about Grandma's kitchen. Couldn't shake it all morning.
My oldest friend didn't come to my birthday and didn't text. Maybe we've just drifted. That's what hurts.
Clearing out the nursery we never used. Folded every tiny onesie and put them in a box for the charity shop.
The vet says Bruno has a few weeks left. He's still wagging. I'm not ready.
Saw an old photo of me and Nikhil at uni and realised I don't even have his number anymore.
Everyone at the party seemed to be having a great time and I just felt far away from all of it. Left early.
Mama's memory is going faster now. She called me by my aunt's name twice today and I just said yes.
Isabel moved her things out today. The bookshelf looks like a mouth with missing teeth.
First Christmas without Papa. We set his place at the table without saying anything. Nobody could eat much.
My manuscript came back with a form rejection. Forty-one now. Some days I can laugh about it. Not today.
I miss who I was before all this. More confident, more fun. I don't know where she went.
Cleaned out my email and found the last message from Theo before the accident. Didn't open it. Couldn't delete it either.
The old dog next door, the one who always barked hello, wasn't at the gate today. Mrs. Bello told me he died on Friday.
Sadness today, low and constant like background music. I did my work. I fed myself. That's all.
Sorting Granny's recipe cards. Her handwriting gets shakier year by year through the box. That got me.
Mateus forgot my birthday. Small thing. Didn't feel small.
Hearing about the floods back home and not being able to do anything from here. Called everyone. They're safe but the village is underwater.
I gave away my piano today because there's no room in the new flat. Watched it go down the stairs on its side like a wounded animal.
Long call with Oyelaran. His divorce is final. He sounded so tired. I felt heavy for him all evening.
I'm grieving a version of my career that's never going to happen. That's the honest sentence.
The hospital let us say goodbye to Aunt Mei. Her hand was so small. I sang her the song she taught me.
Dropped Chloe at college. Her room at home looks huge and empty. I made tea for two out of habit.
Visiting hours over. Waved at Baba through the glass until the nurse closed the curtain.
The shop is closing for good. Three generations. I signed the last lease papers and Dimitri hugged me in the empty storeroom.
Found out Gabe has been unwell for months and didn't tell any of us. I wish he'd let us help.
Watching the leaves fall and thinking about how fast this year went and how little of it I really lived.
Ifeoma's text: 'we lost the baby'. I don't know what to say to her. I've typed and deleted six messages.
Mass at the old church for Señora Ruiz. Half the town came. Everyone has a story of her feeding them.
I think Hamza and I are growing apart and neither of us wants to say it first.
Just a melancholy evening. Old songs, rain, missing people.
Wiktoria's last shift at the hospital before she retires. I've worked beside her for nine years. The ward will feel wrong without her.
Today my son said he's too old for bedtime stories. I said okay and put the book back on the shelf very carefully.
Got the call that Olu's surgery didn't work. They're moving to comfort care.
Missing the person I was in Lisbon. Free and brave and twenty-three.
Biopsy results come back Thursday. I've checked the portal eleven times today even though I know they won't be there yet.
Presentation to the board tomorrow. Stomach in knots. Rehearsed it four times and still feel like I'll forget everything.
Rent went up again and my hours got cut. Did the maths three times. It doesn't work.
Heart racing on the tube for no reason. Got off two stops early and walked. Felt silly but better.
Manager put a 'quick chat' in my calendar for Friday with no details. Now I can't think about anything else.
Couldn't sleep. Lay there replaying the thing I said at dinner and whether Liam thought it was rude.
Exam results open at 9. It's 6:40. I've been awake since 4.
Bit jittery today. Too much coffee or too much going on, hard to say.
I have to tell Joaquín about the money I lost on that investment. I've rehearsed it in the shower all week.
The baby has a fever and it's 2am. Called the nurse line. Waiting for them to call back. Every minute feels like ten.
Awake at 3am thinking about climate stuff, the future, whether it's fair to have kids. Big spiral.
Tax deadline is Friday and the shoebox of receipts is still a shoebox.
Flying on Saturday. I'm the person gripping the armrest at every bump. Already dreading it.
Got a letter from the council about 'planning concerns'. Haven't opened it yet. It's sitting on the table like a bomb.
Chest tight all day. Kept telling myself it's anxiety not my heart. Then worrying it IS my heart. Fun loop.
Meeting Sam's parents this weekend. What do I wear. What do I bring. What if they hate me.
Hearing that sound again in the walls at night. Probably pipes. I've got the light on anyway.
Grandad fell again. He says he's fine. He said that last time too. I'm going over tomorrow to look properly.
Auditions at ten. Voice feels scratchy. Drinking honey water like a Victorian opera singer.
Bank flagged a weird transaction. Spent an hour on hold. Card's frozen. Still not sure what else they got.
Leading my first workshop on Wednesday. Thirty people. Practising in front of the mirror and hating my voice.
Kemi's flight from Lagos is delayed with no update. The board just says 'see agent'. There is no agent.
Phone rang from an unknown number three times. I don't pick up unknown numbers. Now I'm convinced something's happened.
I think I upset Mira in the group chat. She went quiet after my joke. Typed an apology, deleted it, typed it again.
Court date for the custody hearing is next month. I'm trying to keep things normal for the kids but I'm shaking inside.
My hands go numb when I think about the money conversation with Dev. We have to have it. Tonight.
Interview went fine I think? But they said they'd be in touch 'by end of week' and it's Thursday afternoon.
Tornado warning siren went off. We sat in the basement with the radio for an hour. All clear now but I can't settle.
Nervous. Big day tomorrow. Laid my clothes out like a kid before the first day of school.
Can't stop worrying about Lukas. He's been drinking more since the job went and he laughs it off when I ask.
Driving on the motorway for the first time since the accident. Made it. Hands were slippery on the wheel the whole way.
My essay is due tomorrow and I've written 200 words of 3000. My heart is pounding every time I look at the clock.
Waiting room. Again. Everyone looks as scared as I feel.
Mortgage approval still 'pending'. If it doesn't come through by the 15th we lose the house we've fallen in love with.
Group project and nobody has done their part. Presentation's Monday. I can feel my jaw clenching.
Third night in a row of nightmares about missing a train. Waking with my heart going like a drum.
The landlord's agent is coming to inspect and the damp patch in the bathroom has spread. I'm sure we'll lose the deposit.
Election night. Refreshing the results page like it changes anything. Can't eat.
Patrick is hiking alone this weekend and his tracker's been showing the same spot for three hours.
Restless and worried all day about the money, the job, my knee, everything at once and nothing in particular.
Quiet morning. Tea by the window, rain on the glass, nowhere to be until noon.
After yoga I felt properly settled for the first time this week. My shoulders came down from my ears.
Walked the dog along the beach at dusk. Just waves and sand and his silly ears flapping. Head clear.
Meditation app said 'notice the breath'. For once I actually did. Ten minutes of nothing in the best way.
Fished with Grandpa Jun at the reservoir. We caught nothing and barely spoke. Perfect.
The big meeting was moved and suddenly my whole day opened up. Felt the tension just drain out.
I thought the conversation with Esther would be hard but we listened to each other and I left feeling steady.
Rowing at 6am, the lake like glass. Moana and I didn't say a word the whole way out.
Knitting while the radio murmured. Lost track of time completely.
After weeks of noise in my head it's finally quiet. I'm not happy exactly. I'm just at ease.
Was expecting to be nervous before the operation but I felt surprisingly calm. The nurse, Bridget, held my hand and talked about her garden.
Sunday at the allotment. Weeding, the robin following me, mug of coffee on the shed step.
Ended the day sitting with Deepa on the balcony, not talking, watching the city lights come on.
Not stressed for once. Work's under control, flat's tidy, nothing urgent.
Swam forty lengths slowly. Counted strokes. Thoughts went smooth like the water.
Evening walk through the woods with Pablo. The light through the pines was gold. We talked softly about nothing.
Cancelled everything and stayed home reading. Didn't feel guilty about it, which is new.
Lay in the hammock and watched clouds. I'm 38 years old. Highly recommend.
The train was delayed and instead of getting cross I just read my book. Growth?
Night shift was slow. Mopped, restocked, chatted with Ahmed about his allotment. Strangely peaceful at 4am.
I let the phone ring out and finished my tea. It can wait. Everything can wait for ten minutes.
I feel balanced lately. Sleep, walks, fewer screens. Noticing it.
After the funeral everyone left and the house went quiet. I made tea and sat with it. Sad, but calm. Ready to rest.
Gentle day. Baked bread, called Auntie Grace, folded laundry in the sun.
Weekend at the cabin with no signal. By day two my brain stopped buzzing.
Watching Hugo sleep on my chest. His tiny breaths. Everything else fades.
Rain cancelled the match so I spent the afternoon doing a jigsaw. Very relaxing actually.
Flat sea, flat sky, me on the paddleboard in the middle. I could've stayed out there forever.
Bedtime routine with the twins went smoothly for once. Stories, songs, lights out. I lay on the floor between their beds until they were asleep.
A quiet, settled feeling all day. The decision's made and I'm at peace with it.
Long drive home on empty roads at night, old radio station, window cracked. Very peaceful.
I'm surprisingly relaxed about the move. Boxes everywhere and I'm just taking it one box at a time.
Wrote a letter to Mum by hand, sealed it, walked it to the post box at sunset. Felt grounded.
Breathed through the urge to reply angrily to Graham's email. Waited an hour. Wrote a polite one. Felt calm and in control.
Stillness. Morning light on the floorboards. Didn't reach for my phone.
Floated in the sea and let the waves rock me. For a while I couldn't remember what I'd been worrying about.
After the argument we both took a breather. Now we're sitting together on the sofa, quiet, okay again.
Siobhan drove an hour in the rain to bring me soup when I was sick. Didn't even come in, just left it on the step with a note.
Thankful for my body today. It carried me up the mountain even though I doubted it.
The nurses on ward 7 were so kind to Dad tonight. One stayed past her shift to sit with him.
Someone paid for my coffee in the queue. Tiny thing. Changed my whole morning.
Mr. Achebe let me pay the rent late without any fuss. I'll remember that.
Grateful list: warm bed, a job I mostly like, Ollie making me laugh at breakfast, the smell of rain.
My therapist, Dana, said 'you did the hard thing'. I'm so thankful I found her.
Called Aunty Funmi to thank her for paying my exam fees years ago. She'd forgotten. I never will.
Thank you, coffee. Thank you, quiet Saturday. Thank you, whoever invented the electric blanket.
Hyejin covered my shift so I could see my son's recital. I owe her big.
Mum and Dad helped with the deposit. I know it was a stretch for them. I keep looking at the keys and thinking of them.
A year sober today. Grateful for the meetings, for Jim my sponsor, and for whoever I was a year ago who decided to try.
The village rallied after the fire. Clothes, food, a place to sleep. I don't know how to repay this.
Thankful for slow mornings and the way the light comes through the kitchen blinds.
I was so scared about the delivery and the midwife, Precious, was a rock. I'll name a plant after her. Maybe the baby.
Appreciating my old school friends tonight. Twenty years and we still show up for each other.
Gran left me her sewing machine. Every time I use it I feel her hands on mine.
The bus driver waited when he saw me running. Made the connection with a minute to spare.
Rashid translated everything for Mum at the hospital so she wasn't lost. He stayed four hours.
My partner took the night feeds all week so I could sleep. Feel human again. Love him so much.
Thankful that the storm missed us. Thinking of the people on the coast who weren't so lucky.
Got through the interview because Leon spent all weekend doing mock questions with me.
So much gratitude for this little flat. Small, damp in the corners, but mine and safe.
A kid at the park helped me find my glasses in the grass. Wouldn't take the reward. Just said 'have a nice day'.
Dad called just to say he's proud of me. He never says that. I'm holding on to it.
Tamsin and Freddie looked after the dog for two weeks and sent daily photos. He's clearly been spoiled.
Thankful my brother answered at 3am. I needed a voice.
Our elderly neighbour, Mrs. Kowalski, brought pierogi for the whole street after the power cut.
The surgeon, Mr. Adebayo, explained everything slowly and drew me a diagram. I felt like a person not a case number.
Thankful for headphones, for trains that run on time, for the sandwich lady who knows my order.
My students made me a card for my last day. 'You made maths not scary.' Kept it in my coat pocket all evening.
Thank god for the emergency plumber who came at midnight. Bless that man.
Feeling grateful but also guilty that Mum gave up so much so I could study here.
Sundar spotted the mistake in my report before it went to the client. Saved my skin.
The cleaner at the station, Dolores, always says good morning like she means it. I told her today how much it helps.
Thankful for this body that is healing, slowly, stubbornly.
Isaac taught me to drive with endless patience, even when I stalled at the same junction eight times.
Everyone at the shelter knew Ruby by name when I went to adopt her. Grateful for the people who took care of her first.
Grateful to be here. Plain as that. Some years I wasn't sure I would be.
Deeply thankful to the stranger who stopped and called the ambulance when I fainted. I never got his name.
My landlady gave us her old sofa when ours broke. 'Better than the dump,' she said. It's lovely.
The interpreter at the asylum hearing made sure every word I said was heard. I hugged her after.
Big thank you to past me for meal-prepping on Sunday. Present me is very tired.
Abuelo held my face and said 'mi orgullo'. I'm grateful I got to hear that before he goes.
Grateful for good friends, cold beer, and the fact that the barbecue didn't set anything on fire.
Third time this week the printer jammed right before a deadline. I wanted to throw it out the window.
Two hours on hold with the airline. Disconnected. Started again.
Asked Calum to take the bins out four times. Bins still in. Calum still on the sofa.
Great, another 'quick' meeting that ran for ninety minutes and decided nothing.
I've rewritten this paragraph eight times and it's still bad. I know what I want to say. Why won't it come out.
The physio said progress will be slow. I knew that. I just hate not being able to run.
Train cancelled, replacement bus took a scenic tour of every village in the county. Home at 10pm.
Javier keeps taking credit for my work in front of the director. I don't know how to call it out without looking petty.
Why do I always freeze up when I'm speaking French with actual French people. I can do it perfectly in my head.
The insurance company 'needs more documents'. They have had every document since March.
Couldn't get the baby to nap. Tried everything. She finally fell asleep at 5:30pm, perfect for ruining tonight.
Wifi keeps dropping during calls. I look like a frozen potato to my clients.
Ugh. Planned a whole day of writing and got nothing done except reorganising my bookshelf.
My knee is still swollen. It's been three weeks. I've done everything the doctor said.
Spent the whole weekend on the furniture flatpack and there's one piece left over and the drawer won't close.
I'm not angry at Nkechi, I'm just frustrated that we keep having the same conversation about money and nothing changes.
Website crashed on launch day. Hundreds of people trying to sign up and getting an error page.
My body won't let me sleep even though I'm exhausted. Lying here doing the maths on how many hours I'll get.
Couldn't figure out the tax form. Called the helpline. They couldn't figure it out either.
Wanted a peaceful Sunday. Got a leaking boiler, a toddler with a cold and a broken umbrella.
Rejected by the gallery again with the same feedback: 'not quite right for us'. What does that mean?
The groceries were delivered to the wrong flat and now I'm making dinner out of crackers and hope.
I keep explaining to my parents that I'm not 'just playing on the computer', it's literally my job.
Exam was nothing like the practice papers. I knew the material and still messed it up.
Three days into the new diet and I ate an entire pack of biscuits in the car. Back to day one.
Hours on hold with the GP surgery, then all the appointments were gone by the time I got through.
I just can't get through to Theo. He nods and then does exactly the opposite.
I hate that I let it get to me. Nita made one little comment and I stewed on it all day.
Landlord still hasn't fixed the mould. Three emails, two calls, a letter. Kids are coughing.
I'm frustrated with how slow this healing is. Physically and the other kind.
Group chat planning a trip: 47 messages, zero decisions. Again.
The software update moved every button I use. Spent half the morning hunting for 'export'.
Long day of nothing working. The oven, the heating, the bus, my brain.
Deliveroo order arrived cold and missing the main thing I ordered. On the one night I didn't want to cook.
Apparently 'urgent' means 'Cormac forgot to tell you about it until today'.
The new hire keeps asking me questions he could just google. I'm happy to help but I have my own work.
Spent my day off fixing someone else's mistake. Again.
Lost the bid by one vote. Three months of work. They picked the cheaper, worse plan.
I tried to talk to Pilar about how I've been feeling and she turned it into a story about herself.
Every form wants a utility bill and I don't have one in my name because I just moved. Catch-22.
The bread didn't rise. Again. I followed the recipe to the gram.
We booked Japan!!! Flights in April. I've already made a spreadsheet of ramen shops.
Starting the new job on Monday. Can't stop thinking about all the things I'll get to build.
Concert tomorrow! Front row! Bea and I have matching shirts ready.
Puppy comes home Saturday. Bought a bed, a lead, eleven toys. I have a problem.
Two days until I see Malik after eight months apart. I'm counting hours.
First seeds of the year went in today. Already imagining the summer salad.
The band said yes, I can join as their drummer! First rehearsal Thursday.
Can't sleep, too buzzed about the hackathon. We have the idea. We have the team. Let's go.
We find out the baby's sex next week. Leaning towards not finding out but I'm so curious.
Mohammed got us tickets to the cup final!! I'm going to lose my voice.
Got invited to speak at the conference in Berlin. Me! Up on a stage!
Christmas Eve buzz. Lights on, cookies in the oven, Leo can't sit still and honestly neither can I.
Bought my first camera. Going out at sunrise tomorrow to shoot the harbour.
Last day of exams tomorrow and then SUMMER. Freedom.
Course starts in October and I've already read half the reading list. Nerd and proud.
The festival line-up dropped and every band I love is playing. Bought tickets in four minutes.
Tomorrow I start learning to dive. Open water by the end of the week if the instructor, Mika, thinks I'm ready.
Gig at the pub on Friday. Our first ever with people who aren't related to us.
Telescope arrived! Clear skies tonight. Saturn, here I come.
Yesterday felt flat but today I've got that fizzy feeling about the trip again.
Orientation week! So many clubs. Signed up for climbing, debate and something called 'competitive cheese tasting'.
Mira said she might be pregnant. Test tomorrow morning. We're trying not to get our hopes up and absolutely getting our hopes up.
The kitchen renovation starts Monday. Goodbye 1970s brown tiles!
Getting my first tattoo on Saturday. Designed it myself. Zahra's coming to hold my hand.
Countdown to the eclipse: four days. We're driving to the path of totality and I have the special glasses.
First home game of the season tonight. Scarf on since breakfast.
Applying for the master's programme and actually excited for the first time in ages about what's next.
Can't wait for Diwali at Nani's. Lamps, sweets, all the cousins in one house.
Got a callback for the second audition!!! Callbacks are Wednesday.
Bought the paints, cleared the table, the course starts tonight. I've wanted to try oils since I was a teenager.
Interview at my dream company next week. Practising answers and getting more excited than nervous, which is new.
Harvest festival planning with the whole street. Jean-Luc's doing a cider press. I'm on bunting.
We close on the house on Friday! Our own front door!
Tomorrow is the first day of my sabbatical. A whole year to write. I keep grinning at nothing.
Tickets for the musical go on sale at 10. Alarm set. Three devices ready. Ellen is on standby.
The kittens open their eyes any day now. Checking on them every hour like a nervous grandma.
Dad is finally coming to visit me abroad. Planning everything I want to show him.
Feeling a spark about the business idea again. Stayed up sketching until 2am.
Our first holiday as a family of four. Suitcases on the bed. Kids already wearing swimsuits indoors.
The test print of my zine came out beautifully. Launch party next month!
Almost done with the renovation. Floors go in tomorrow. Can practically taste the housewarming.
Bubbling with ideas after the workshop. Filled ten pages of my notebook on the train home.
Finally get my cast off on Thursday. Planning my first swim already.
The garden show is this weekend and my dahlias are blooming at exactly the right time.
Packed for the Arctic trip three days early. Checked the aurora forecast twenty times.
Lunch with Ines on Friday to plan the business properly. Feels real now.
Started learning Spanish with an app and I want to practise all the time. Ordering coffee in Spanish next month in Seville!
Thinking about how I used to measure a good day by how much I got done. Lately it's more about whether I was kind.
Wondering whether I avoid conflict because I'm peaceful or because I'm scared. Probably both.
What would I do if money didn't matter? Same job, I think, fewer hours. That's useful to know.
Mum and I talked about her childhood today. Some of my habits make more sense now.
Is ambition something I actually want or something I absorbed? Turning that over all evening.
Funerals make you think. Listening to the speeches for Mr. Ito I wondered what people would say about me.
Long walk, long think. Not sad, not happy, just sorting through things.
The argument with Jonas was about the dishes on the surface. Underneath it's about feeling unseen. Need to say that next time.
Sat in the old school car park and remembered being fourteen and so sure everyone hated me. Wish I could tell her it gets better.
Thinking about forgiveness. I don't think I need to forgive Callum to move on. I just need to stop carrying it.
Six months of therapy. Biggest lesson so far: feelings aren't facts.
What I'd tell my younger self: rest is not laziness. Ask the question. Wear the coat.
Did I move abroad to find something or to escape something? Five years in, I think the answer was escape, and then it became find.
Quiet evening going through photos from the year. More happy moments than I remembered.
Talking with Bilal about faith made me realise mine changed shape rather than disappeared.
I keep saying I want a quieter life and then saying yes to everything. Interesting contradiction.
Wondering what home means now. The house where I grew up is sold. My flat feels temporary. Maybe it's people, not places.
Birthday thoughts at 50: fewer things, more people, better shoes.
Looked at the job description I wrote for myself last year. I've grown into it more than I expected.
I've been thinking about why the comment from Priyanka stung so much. It touched something I already believe about myself.
Spent the evening thinking about what I actually want from a partner, not what looks good on paper.
Pondering the idea that rest is something you plan, not something you earn.
I think the reason I keep busy is that stillness lets the grief in. Writing that down feels important.
Watched the documentary about my hometown and saw it through outsiders' eyes. It's smaller and kinder than I remember.
Every year I write the same goals. Maybe they're not goals. Maybe they're values I already have and just want to notice.
Grandma's diary from 1962 arrived from the attic. She worried about the same things I worry about. Money, love, being enough.
Thinking about how much of my personality is just my mother's anxieties in a nicer outfit.
Conversation with Elena on the train about regret. She says she regrets nothing. I regret a few things and I'm okay with that.
I'm not upset about the promotion going to Shreya. It just made me ask whether I wanted it at all.
Hard to know if I'm growing apart from the old crowd or growing into myself. Same thing maybe.
Spent the morning sorting old notebooks. My handwriting changed when Dad died. I never noticed until today.
Talked with Uncle Femi about the war. He spoke for an hour and then said 'that's enough for one day'. Thinking about it still.
First anniversary of moving in with Nico. Learned a lot about compromise. And towels. So many opinions about towels.
Visited the old flat. New family, new paint. I stood across the road and remembered all of it, the good and the awful.

Then at the point where I fell last time I froze, and the old panic came up my throat. I breathed. I looked at my feet. I made the move. I got to the top of a route a child could climb and I sat at the top crying a bit. Sol was below grinning. I'm so proud of myself I could burst.

Sunday, and the whole family came for lunch for the first time since Nonna's funeral. I was worried it would be sad, that we'd all sit around her empty chair and not know what to say. Instead Zio Franco told the story about Nonna chasing the priest out of the kitchen with a wooden spoon, and everyone laughed until they cried, and then just cried, and then laughed again. My niece Bianca made the gnocchi using Nonna's recipe and they were lumpy and perfect. We stayed at the table until it was dark. Nobody wanted to clear the plates. Driving home I felt full in every sense, grateful that we still have each other and still have her, in the stories and the recipes and the noise.

I want to write down how the day actually went because I keep telling people 'fine'. Woke up at five with the baby. Fed her, changed her, she was sick on both of us, changed us both. Kwesi left at seven for his shift. By nine I'd had half a coffee and no breakfast. The health visitor came at eleven and I'd forgotten, so she found me in yesterday's T-shirt surrounded by washing. She was kind about it. In the afternoon the baby cried for two hours straight and I cried with her for some of it. I love her so much it scares me and I'm so tired I can feel my heartbeat in my eyes. Kwesi got home at eight and took her and I fell asleep sitting up on the sofa. That's the day. Not fine. But we're alive and fed and that's something.

I'm writing this on the train back from the hospital and I'm so angry I can barely hold the pen. They discharged Dad yesterday even though he could hardly stand, because they 'needed the bed'. No care plan, no follow-up, a bag of pills and a leaflet. Last night he fell in the bathroom and lay there for two hours before the neighbour heard him. Now he's back in A&E with a fractured hip and the same doctor who discharged him is acting like it's bad luck. It isn't bad luck. It's a system that treats old people like parcels. I made a formal complaint and the woman at the desk sighed at me like I was the problem. I wanted to scream at someone and there was nobody to scream at who deserved it.

Long walk with Zeynep along the cliffs. We set out meaning to talk about her wedding plans and ended up talking about everything else: our mothers, her doubts about her job, my doubts about everything, the way the sea looks different every single time. At one point we sat on a bench with a plaque for someone who 'loved this view' and didn't say anything for a while. Then a gull stole her sandwich and we laughed so hard a passing couple stopped to ask if we were okay. I came home sunburnt and windswept and lighter than I've felt in months. There's nothing like a friend who has known you for twenty years and still wants to hear what you think.

It's three in the morning and the house is silent and I feel calm in a way I haven't for months. The decision is made. I'm leaving the band. We talked it through tonight, all four of us, around the kitchen table at Ines's place, and it was sad and honest and nobody was cruel. They understand. I'll still help with the album, I'll play the last gig in December, and after that I'm going to try being someone who has weekends. I thought I'd feel panic or grief. Instead there's this long exhale. I've been carrying the guilt of wanting out for a year. Now it's said out loud, and the world didn't end. I'm going to sleep well tonight.

Second Christmas in this city and I spent it mostly on my own again. I had the invitation from Hiroshi's family but I said I was busy, because I couldn't face being the extra person at someone else's table, smiling through jokes I don't understand. So I cooked a small meal, watched the old films my dad used to love, and called home at the hour when everyone there was already half asleep. My sister passed the phone around and I heard the noise of the house, the dog, my nephew shouting about a present. When I hung up the silence in the flat was so complete I could hear the fridge. I keep telling myself next year will be different, that I'll have made more friends by then. I said that last year too. I'm tired of being the person who doesn't belong anywhere.

Sunday, and I spent the whole of it doing almost nothing, which is exactly what I needed. Slept until nine, made a proper breakfast with eggs and the good bread, then sat in the garden with the paper while Marcus fiddled with the lawnmower and swore at it gently. In the afternoon we walked up the hill behind the village and back, slowly, stopping to look at the sheep and the view of the reservoir. Nothing special happened and nobody needed anything from me. I didn't check my work email once. Dinner was leftovers. Now the light is fading, the cat is asleep on my feet and there's a film on that neither of us is really watching. I feel full up in a quiet way, like everything is where it should be. I'd like more Sundays like this one.

I sat by the canal for an hour after work today and let my mind go blank in a way that hasn't happened in months. The water was flat and green, a heron was standing on the far bank so still I thought it was a sculpture until it moved, and every so often a narrowboat chugged past with someone waving from the back. I watched the light change on the brick of the old warehouses. I didn't think about the project or the mortgage or the argument with my brother. I just sat. When I got up my legs were stiff and the air had gone cool and I realised I hadn't looked at my phone once. I walked home slowly. I want to remember that this is available to me, ten minutes from my front door, whenever I need it.

I gave my first full lecture today, an hour long, to a hall of about a hundred and twenty first-year students, and I didn't fall apart. I'd rehearsed it so many times that Amira can probably recite it, and I was still convinced I'd freeze or my slides would break or someone would ask a question I couldn't answer. In the end the projector worked, I made a joke that actually landed, and three students stayed behind to ask about the reading. One of them said it was the first lecture this term she'd actually understood. Walking back across the campus I felt about ten feet tall. Two years ago I couldn't speak in a seminar of eight people without my voice shaking. I know it's only one lecture and there are twenty more to go, but I did it, and I did it well.

During the day I do the washing in between feeds and forget to eat until the afternoon. My mother visits and tells me to sleep when the baby sleeps, which is lovely advice from someone who has not met this baby. I love her completely and fiercely and I am so tired that I put the milk in the cupboard and the cereal in the fridge this morning and didn't notice until lunch. My eyes ache. My bones ache. I'm going to try to sleep now.

I think I've been depressed for a while and only now have the words for it. Looking back over these pages, the last two months are full of entries that say 'tired', 'flat', 'couldn't be bothered', and I just thought it was the winter. I stopped going to choir. I stopped calling Bea back. I've eaten toast for dinner most nights. Today I couldn't make myself get out of bed until eleven, and when I did I sat on the edge of it for twenty minutes. I'm not in danger, I want to be clear about that, I'm just grey all the way through. I've booked a GP appointment for Thursday, which took everything I had. Writing this down is the first honest thing I've done in weeks. I want to feel like myself again. I'm not sure I remember how.

Long day at the allotment and I'm writing this with soil still under my fingernails. The broad beans are finally up, the onions look strong, and the rhubarb that Mr. Patel gave me as a cutting two years ago has gone completely wild. We shared a flask of tea on the bench between our plots and he told me about the garden his father kept in Gujarat, mangoes and chillies and a well he used to drop stones into as a boy. I told him about my grandmother's roses. Neither of us said much after that, we just sat and looked at our rows. On the walk home I felt properly content, the kind of tired that comes from using your body for something. Dinner was new potatoes from the plot with butter and salt. Nothing better.

I keep thinking about my twenties and how sure I was that I'd have it all worked out by forty. Well, I'm forty now. I've had three careers, one marriage, two cities, a lot of therapy and a dog. I'm not where I planned to be. I don't own a house. I don't run a company. But I wake up most days and like the person I am, which younger me would have found impossible to believe. She hated herself quite a lot. Somewhere along the way, through the divorce and the redundancy and the long slow work of being honest with people, I became someone gentler. I'm writing this down because my birthday dinner is tomorrow and everyone will ask what I'm proud of, and I want an answer that isn't a job title. Maybe this is it.

Tomorrow is the day. After two years of training, endless blisters, the stress fracture, the month of physio and all those dark mornings, I'm running the London marathon. My kit is laid out on the bed like a crime scene: shorts, vest with my name on, gels, plasters, the lucky socks Ayo gave me. I've checked the route map four times and the weather forecast eleven times. My parents are driving down at dawn to stand at mile eighteen with a sign. I keep picturing turning onto the Mall and seeing the finish line, and every time I do my stomach flips with nerves and excitement in equal parts. I know it's going to hurt. I know I might have to walk. I don't care. I've been waiting for this for so long. I'll never sleep tonight.

I don't know how to describe this week except that I have been carrying too many things for too many people and something has to give. Dad's care package collapsed on Monday when the agency lost two carers, so I've been driving over every morning before work and every evening after. Work has a major release on Friday and my team is two people down. Ellie has exams and needs help with revision, and Sam's football has been moved to the other side of town. The house is chaos, the fridge is empty, the cat has been sick twice. I made a list tonight and it has forty-two items on it. I read it through and then just put my head down on the kitchen table for a while. I don't even know which thing to start with. All of it, apparently.

Living alone was supposed to feel like freedom, and in the daytime it mostly does. I like choosing what to eat and when to sleep and leaving my books in piles. But the evenings are long now that the clocks have gone back. I come home at six to a dark flat, put the lamps on, make dinner for one and eat it in front of a screen. Sometimes I realise I haven't said a single word out loud since leaving work. I've started talking to the plants, which is either charming or a warning sign. Laura and the others from university all live in other cities now, with partners and babies and lives that fill up their weekends. We message, but it's not the same as having someone drop round. I don't need a crowd. I'd just like one person nearby.

I wanted to record this before it fades. This evening, completely out of the blue, my old teacher Mr. Hassan emailed me. He'd seen the article about the charity in the local paper and wanted to say that he'd always known I'd do something like this. He remembered things I'd forgotten, like the time I organised a bake sale for the flood appeal when I was twelve, and how I used to argue with him about everything in class. He said I was 'difficult in the best way'. I sat at the kitchen table and cried, because when I was at that school I felt like nobody noticed me at all. It turns out someone did. I wrote back for an hour. I'm going to visit him when I'm next home. I'm so grateful he took the time.

Something shifted this week and I want to notice it. For months the grief over Mum has been like weather I couldn't predict, rolling in at the supermarket or in the car or halfway through a meeting. This week it came more gently. I made her lemon cake on Sunday and instead of crying into the bowl I found myself smiling at the memory of her licking the spoon and pretending she hadn't. On Wednesday a song of hers came on the radio and I sang along. I still miss her every day. But I can feel the edges softening, and I can picture a future where she's a warm presence in the background of my life rather than an open wound. Rhiannon, my counsellor, said this might happen. I didn't believe her. I'm starting to now.

I am still furious about what happened at the parents' meeting tonight. The head announced, as if it were good news, that the school is cutting the special needs support assistants from six to two because of the budget. Two. For four hundred children. When I put my hand up and asked how my daughter, who has one-to-one support in her statement, will get the help she is legally entitled to, he said they would 'explore creative solutions'. Several parents clapped him. Clapped. I walked out because I could feel myself about to say something unforgivable. I've drafted an email to the governors, a letter to the local councillor, and a post for the parents' group. I'll send them in the morning when I've calmed down enough to spell properly. My daughter deserves better than creative solutions.

I finally finished the novel. Nine years, four complete rewrites, two agents who said no, one long period where I didn't open the file at all, and a lot of very early mornings at the kitchen table before work. Tonight at eleven I typed the last sentence, sat back, and read it aloud to the empty room. Then I printed the whole thing, all three hundred and twelve pages, just so I could hold it. It's sitting on the table next to me now in a slightly crooked pile. I don't know if anyone will ever publish it. I don't even know if it's good. But it exists, and it exists because I kept going when every sensible part of me wanted to stop. I'm prouder of this than of anything else I've ever done. I'm going to open a bottle of something.

I cleared my calendar for the whole of today and didn't tell anyone, which I've never done before. I turned my phone off at nine and left it in a drawer. I walked to the bakery for a cinnamon bun, then sat in the window of the café with a notebook and wrote whatever came into my head for an hour. In the afternoon I took the bus to the botanical gardens and wandered the glasshouses, reading the little signs about each plant. I sat by the pond for a long time watching the koi. Nobody needed anything from me. No decisions, no problems, no messages. Coming home I felt lighter and slower, like the whole of me had been put back in the right order. I didn't realise how loud my life had become until I turned it off for a day.

Lockdown memories came back today out of nowhere. I was clearing out a drawer and found the little notebook where I used to tick off the days we didn't leave the flat. Ninety-three ticks. I remember how quiet the street was, the clapping on Thursdays, the way Aiden and I learned to make bread badly and argued about who used the last of the flour. I remember being frightened for Mum in the care home and not being able to visit, talking to her through a window. It feels like another life. Sitting on the floor with that notebook I felt a strange mix of things, sadness for that version of us, relief it's over, and something like tenderness for how hard we all tried to keep going. I put the notebook back in the drawer. I'm not ready to throw it away.

This is the longest I've been on a waiting list for anything and the frustration is starting to eat at me. Eighteen months ago my GP referred me to the rheumatology clinic because of the joint pain. Since then I have had one letter confirming the referral, one letter saying the waiting time is 'currently longer than usual', and three phone calls where I was told I'm 'in the system'. Meanwhile my hands hurt every morning, I've stopped playing the piano, and I've had to ask Ravi to open jars for me like I'm ninety. I'm forty-four. I've tried going private but it's two hundred pounds just for a first appointment. Every time I ring, the receptionist is perfectly nice and completely unable to help. I'm not angry with her. I'm angry with all of it.

Eleven days until the move to Edinburgh and I'm buzzing in a way I haven't been in years. I've started packing the books, which in my case means packing about thirty boxes and arguing with myself about every single novel. I've found a café near the new flat that does the kind of strong coffee I like. I've joined the climbing gym online already and signed up for a beginner's Gaelic class just because I can. Rana is driving up with me and we've planned a stop in York for the night. I know there'll be hard days, a new job, no friends at first, the dark winters everyone warns me about. But right now all I can feel is that something new is about to begin, and I've been ready for something new for a very long time. Counting down.

The house has been quiet since the kids went back to university and I keep finding things that make me stop. Jas's hoodie on the back of the kitchen chair. A note from Kiran on the fridge saying 'buy more cereal pls'. The extra mugs in the dishwasher that I no longer need to use. I'm proud of them, I'm glad they're out there living, and the house is very empty. Dinner for two feels strange after twenty years of cooking for four. Raj and I sat at the table tonight and didn't quite know what to talk about without the kids' chaos to fill the gaps. We laughed about it eventually. I think we'll find our way back to being just us. But tonight the quiet is loud, and I miss the noise more than I expected.

I finished my first year of sobriety today, and I want to write down something other than the number. A year ago I couldn't get through an evening without a bottle and I'd stopped answering the door. I'd missed my niece's christening and lied about why. I'd lost the job, and nearly lost Hana. This year I've been to three hundred and twelve meetings, learned to cook, started running, apologised to the people I hurt, and watched my sponsor, Pete, get his ten-year chip. Hana and I are rebuilding, slowly, carefully. I still want a drink most evenings around six. I just don't have one. Tonight we're having dinner at the little Italian place where we had our first date. I'm proud of myself in a way that I don't need anyone else to approve of.

Called the plumber about the dripping tap; he's coming Wednesday morning. Sorted the recycling. Early night planned. That's the whole day, written down so I remember when things were done.
